# Overlapping histograms {#sec-overlapping-histograms} ::: {.callout-tip appearance='simple' icon=false} ***This graph is largely complete and just needs final proof reading.*** ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}
::: {.cell layout-align="right"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](overlapping_histograms_files/figure-html/full_code_display-1.png){fig-align='right' width=60% height=60%} ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"} **Requirements:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a categorical variable** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a numeric (continuous) variable** ::: :::: ## Description Overlapping histograms allow us to compare distributions across the groups of a categorical (or ordinal) variable. ## Set up ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **PACKAGES:** ::: Install packages. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DATA:** ::: In 1997, kids everywhere were feeding, cleaning, and playing with Tamagotchis, and how long a virtual pet lived depended on how well it was cared for. We'll simulate the lifespans of 450 pets, 150 for each level of care. `rweibull()` draws each lifespan from a Weibull distribution, and the `scale` for each level of care (6, 13, or 21 days) stretches the lifespans of better cared for pets. Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 450 pets every time you run the code below. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} set.seed(1997) tamagotchi_pets <- tibble( pet_id = 1:450, care = rep(c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered"), each = 150)) |> mutate(care = factor(care, levels = c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered")), lifespan_days = round(rweibull(n(), shape = 2.2, scale = c(Neglected = 6, Average = 13, Pampered = 21)[as.character(care)]), 1)) glimpse(tamagotchi_pets) #> Rows: 450 #> Columns: 3 #> $ pet_id 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9,… #> $ care Neglected, Neglected, Negl… #> $ lifespan_days 7.2, 4.2, 2.9, 3.3, 8.2, 4… ``` ::: ::: ## Distribution Overlapping histograms compare the shape of one variable across groups. Here the groups have the same *kind* of shape (they all come from the same distribution), but each one is stretched by a different amount. Below we'll move from the pets, to a picture, to the formula. ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **COUNT IT:** ::: Start with the first five pets (all neglected). ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} head(tamagotchi_pets, 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: None of these neglected pets made it past nine days. The summary below compares the three levels of care. Each mean is a little higher than its median, and the longest lived pet in each group lasted more than twice as long as the median. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} tamagotchi_pets |> group_by(care) |> summarise( mean = mean(lifespan_days), median = median(lifespan_days), max = max(lifespan_days)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DRAW IT:** ::: The histograms below are drawn on top of each other (`position = "identity"`), and the lines are the Weibull curves we drew the lifespans from, scaled to match the counts. Every group has the same lopsided hump with a tail to the right. Better care doesn't change the shape; it stretches the hump to the right and flattens it out. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} weibull_curves <- tidyr::expand_grid( care = factor(c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered"), levels = c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered")), lifespan_days = seq(0, 45, by = 0.25)) |> mutate(scale = c(Neglected = 6, Average = 13, Pampered = 21)[as.character(care)], count = 150 * (45 / 40) * dweibull(lifespan_days, shape = 2.2, scale = scale)) ggplot(data = tamagotchi_pets, aes(x = lifespan_days, fill = care)) + geom_histogram(alpha = 2/3, position = "identity", binwidth = 45 / 40, boundary = 0) + geom_line(data = weibull_curves, aes(y = count, color = care), linewidth = 1, show.legend = FALSE) + labs(x = "Lifespan (days)", y = "Pets", fill = "Care") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](overlapping_histograms_files/figure-html/draw_ovrlp_hist-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **NAME IT:** ::: The [Weibull distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weibull_distribution) is a common model for lifetimes. It has a shape ($k$) and a scale ($\lambda$): $$ X \sim \text{Weibull}(k = 2.2, \; \lambda_{\text{care}}), \quad \lambda = (6, 13, 21) $$ The chance that a pet is still alive after $t$ days is $e^{-(t/\lambda)^k}$. When the shape is greater than 1 (like our 2.2), the risk of a pet dying grows the longer it lives, which gives the histogram its hump and right tail. The scale stretches everything: the median lifespan is $\lambda (\ln 2)^{1/k}$, which is about 5, 11, and 18 days for our three groups. Our simulated medians are 5.3, 10.8, 18 days. Try changing `shape` in `rweibull()`. A shape of 1 turns the hump into a steady decline (pets die at the same rate no matter their age), and a large shape makes every pet in a group die at about the same time. ## Grammar ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CODE:** ::: - Create labels with `labs()` - Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data` - Map `lifespan_days` to the `x` axis and `care` to `fill` - Inside `geom_histogram()`, set `alpha` to `2/3`, `position` to `"identity"` (so the bars overlap instead of stacking), and `bins` to `40` ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} labs_ovrlp_hist <- labs( title = "Tamagotchi lifespans", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "450 virtual pets and how they were cared for", x = "Lifespan (days)", fill = "Care") ggp2_ovrlp_hist <- ggplot(data = tamagotchi_pets, aes(x = lifespan_days, fill = care)) + geom_histogram(alpha = 2/3, position = "identity", bins = 40) ggp2_ovrlp_hist + labs_ovrlp_hist ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column-margin} Experiment with different `binwidth`s when comparing distributions across groups. ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **GRAPH:** ::: Histograms work by dividing the variable provided to `x` [*into bins and counting the number of observations in each bin.*](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_histogram.html) ::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](overlapping_histograms_files/figure-html/create_graph_ovrlp_hist-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: :::
